chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
title: Hemp Pie and other musicians from Pittsburgh and the Midwest
summary: She lists Pittsburgh figures such as George Benson and musicians from Ohio, Detroit and Chicago.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: I think the Philadelphians have probably found themselves teamed up together on record more than people from other cities with the exception of Detroit, I guess.

I don't know, I mean Pittsburgh, I don't know that they're in the business of - you had to come to New York to make a record so you had to go someplace else, you know. There's a lot of talent around Pittsburgh that should have been on records that never made it. They just didn't want to leave. I think some of the musicians, I'm not sure who, I think several musicians came to New York and appeared with the Savoy Sultons but they didn't stay. I think Hen Pie came, who
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

I was telling you about previously, came to New York and worked with the Savoy Sultons for awhile. He was very good. And Paul Thomas, the trumpet player I was telling you about, working with Harry and Harry's band, a very good trumpet player. The musicians were really great and they was playing some good arrangements too. It would have been nice if that band could have come to New York with me, but by that time I was not even affiliated with the band anymore. I think Harry had given up his band anyway.
Yeah, I've just been looking in the index of Albert McCarthy's book on Big Band Jazz in case that nickname turns up there.

Yes, Hemp Pie. I don't know what Hempie's last name was. It was a very good tenor man and as I said before, Harry had practically given up his band by the time I came to New York. You know, for some reason or other the musicians from Pittsburgh, if they come to New York, they don't stay. They don't like it. They go back. But as I said before there's an awful lot of talent around Pittsburgh. There still is, you know. What's the young guitar player's name that
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

just came out of Pittsburgh, George Benson. And of course [Errol] must have been a baby when I was at Pittsburgh. And of course, I knew Linton Garner, his brother. I worked on Bill with him several times when he was accompanying Timmy Rodgers, the comedian.
Yeah, I think he did some arranging for one of the Ekstine Bands.
And he lived by Montreal for some years.

Yes, I know. Quite talented family. And there was a very famous musician, more of a serious musician, Mary Lucinda Cauldwell who was responsible for a lot of the young musicians getting their early education in Pittsburgh. I suppose the musicians said, why come to New York? Pittsburgh was big enough for them and to become a member of an orchestra in Pittsburgh was no small thing. It's just like any other town, Cleveland, Ohio, and Chicago, Detroit, they all have their local bands, good bands.
Yes, although Chicago has been a place where musicians have migrated to.

You know, almost like New York in that respect.
Yeah, more or less. And a lot of musicians from around Ohio and Detroit, they would be inclined to migrate to Chicago or Pittsburgh. A lot of musicians come to Pittsburgh from Ohio.
Well, Billy Strayhorn who lived in the City for some period of his life before he met Duke Ellington. He was born in Dayton, Ohio.
Yeah, yeah, sure. Cleveland used to turn out quite a few good musicians.
